In the book of Ibn 'Aṭiyya: "Nāfi' recited ﴿Nay, but rān﴾ without assimilation." And in it also: "Nāfi' also recited with assimilation and imāla." Sībawayh said: with a lām followed by a rā', as in (asfalu raḥimihi), both clarification (bayān) and assimilation (idghām) are good. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It was read with assimilation of the lām into the rā' and with clarification; the assimilation is better, and the alif was inclined (imāla) and emphasized (tafkhīm)." End of quotation. Sībawayh also said: when the lām is not the lām of definiteness, as the lām of (hal) and (bal), assimilation in some of them is better, such as (hal ra'ayta); if you do not assimilate and say (hal ra'ayta), it is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, which is rare but permissible. End of quotation.

Al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī said: it is sin upon sin. Al-Ḥasan said: until his heart dies. Al-Suddī said: until the heart turns black. A ḥadīth similar to this is also reported. Al-Kalbī said: He sealed (ṭaba'a) upon their hearts. Ibn Salām said: He covered them.

**﴿what they used to earn﴾**: Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: He attached the blame to them for what they earned, even though that occurs by creation and origination from Him, Exalted is He, because reward and punishment are tied to the servant's acquisition (kasb). The pronoun in His words **(innahum)** refers to the disbelievers. Whoever holds the view of seeing (Allah), which is the position of the People of the Sunnah, says that these will not see their Lord; they are veiled from Him. Mālik used this verse as evidence for the view of seeing by way of the indication of the discourse (dalīl al-khiṭāb), since if He veiled all, this specification would not be meaningful. Al-Shāfi'ī said: Since He veiled a people by displeasure, it indicates that another people will see Him with good pleasure. Whoever holds that there is no seeing, which is the position of the Mu'tazilah, says: they will be veiled from their Lord and His forgiveness. End of quotation. Anas ibn Mālik said: When He veiled His enemies so that they did not see Him, He manifested Himself to His friends until they saw Him. A poet said:

*When they approach the gate of a man of reproach, they are welcomed, while people are divided between one who is welcomed and one who is veiled.*

And from Ibn 'Abbās, Qatādah, and Ibn Abī Mulaykah: veiled from His mercy. And from Ibn Kaysān: from His honor. End of quotation. And from Mujāhid: the meaning is that they are veiled from His honor and His mercy. **(from their Lord)** is attached to **(veiled)**, and it is the governing element of **(yawma'idhin)**. Then, together with being veiled from Allah, they are the burners of the Fire, and this is the fruit of the veil. **﴿Then it will be said﴾**, that is, the keepers of the Fire will say to them: **(this)**, that is, the punishment and the burning of the Fire, and this is **﴿the Day which you used to deny﴾**. His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿No! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾, ﴿And what will make you know what ʿIlliyyūn is?﴾, ﴿A written record﴾, ﴿witnessed by those brought near﴾, ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾, ﴿They are given to drink from a sealed wine﴾, ﴿its seal is musk﴾, ﴿and for that let the competitors compete﴾, ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnīm﴾, ﴿a spring from which those brought near drink﴾, ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾, ﴿and when they passed by them, they would wink at one another﴾, ﴿and when they returned to their people, they returned jesting﴾, ﴿and when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are astray"﴾, ﴿but they were not sent as guardians over them﴾, ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do?﴾.

Al-Farrā' said: it is a noun established in the form of a plural, having no singular from its own form, like ʿishrīn and thalāthīn; when the Arabs form a plural and it has no pattern from its singular or dual, they use the wāw and nūn for both masculine and feminine. Muqātil said: they observe the people of the Fire. It was said: some of them look at others.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī also recited likewise, except that he recited **(yuʿrafu)** with yā', since the feminine marking of **naḍrah** is metaphorical. The meaning of **al-naḍrah** has been explained earlier in His words: ﴿radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insān: 11].

It was said: it is mixed with camphor and its mixture is sealed with musk. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: al-khitām is the clay with which something is sealed. Likewise Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: its vessel was sealed with musk instead of clay. A poet said:

*As if a clear-sparkling wine from Buṣrā, whose scent was carried by the breezes, were tightly sealed.*

[p. 443] The position of the majority is that the righteous are the companions of the right hand, and that those brought near are the foremost. Some people said: the righteous and those brought near in this verse have one meaning, applying to everyone who is given bliss in Paradise.

It is reported that ʿAlī and a group of believers with him passed by a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh, and they laughed at them and mocked them in play. Then the verse was revealed: **﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes﴾**, before ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, reached the Messenger (ﷺ). Abū Rajāʾ, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, Abū Jaʿfar, and Ḥafṣ recited it without alif. The pronoun in the nominative in **(raʾawhum)** refers to the guilty, meaning: when they saw the believers, they attributed them to error, and they were right in attributing it to them.

It was also said: a transparent curtain between them through which they see their condition. **﴿Have they been rewarded?﴾**, that is, were they recompensed? It is said: **thawwaba** and **athāba** when one repays him. From it is the poet's saying:

*I will reward you, or a rewarder on my behalf will reward you, and it is enough for you that you be praised and thanked.*

This is an interrogative with the meaning of confirmation for the believers, meaning: were they recompensed for it? It was also said: **﴿Have they been rewarded?﴾** is attached to **(observing)**, and **(observing)** is governed by the sentence in a position of accusative after dropping the preposition **ilā** ("to"). From al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿĪsā, and Aḥmad ibn Jubayr al-Anṭākī, from al-Kisāʾī: a kasrah on the tā', meaning its last, like His words: ﴿and the Seal of the Prophets﴾. There is an ellipsis in it, meaning: the seal of its fragrance is musk, or its seal with which it is sealed and cut off.

**﴿from Tasnīm﴾**: ʿAbd Allāh and Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is the most noble drink of Paradise, and it is a masculine noun for the water of a spring in Paradise. Al-Zamakhsharī said: **(Tasnīm)** is a proper name for a specific spring, named Tasnīm, which is the verbal noun of sannamahu, meaning "he raised it." **(ʿAynan)** is in the accusative as an expression of praise. Al-Zajjāj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). End of quotation. Al-Akhfash said: they are given to drink a spring (ʿaynan) **﴿from which they drink﴾**, meaning they drink it, or from it; or the verb **(yashrabu)** is implicitly made to mean **(yurwā)**, and about **(bihā)** there are several views. **(those brought near)**: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and Abū Ṣāliḥ said: those brought near drink it pure, and it is mixed for the righteous. [p. 443] The position of the majority is that the righteous are the companions of the right hand, and that those brought near are the foremost. Some people said: the righteous and those brought near in this verse have one meaning, applying to everyone who is given bliss in Paradise.

It is reported that ʿAlī and a group of believers with him passed by a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh, and they laughed at them and mocked them in play. Then the verse was revealed: **﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes﴾**, before ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, reached the Messenger (ﷺ). These disbelievers of Makkah are said to be: Abū Jahl, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, and al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil. The believers are: ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb, Khabbāb, Bilāl, and others of the poor believers. The apparent view is that the pronoun in **(marrū)** refers to **﴿those who committed crimes﴾**, since in that there is consistency of pronouns for one referent. It was also said: it refers to the believers, meaning: when the believers passed by the disbelievers, the disbelievers would wink, that is, indicate with their eyes. **(jesting)**: that is, delighting in mentioning them and in laughing at them. The majority recited **(fākihīn)** with an alif, meaning possessors of jest, play, and joy at their mockery of the people of faith. Abū Rajāʾ, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, Abū Jaʿfar, and Ḥafṣ recited it without alif. The pronoun in the nominative in **(raʾawhum)** refers to the guilty, meaning: when they saw the believers, they attributed them to error, and they were right in attributing it to them.

**﴿but they were not sent﴾** as guardians over the disbelievers. The mention of their being astray is a provocation of speech among them, and there was in the verse some gentleness (muwādaʿah), meaning: the believers were not sent to be guardians over the disbelievers. This is according to the view that this was abrogated by the verse of the sword. Al-Zamakhsharī said: and they were not sent as guardians over them, as a denial of their hindering them from polytheism and of their calling them to Islam and their striving in that. Since the mention of the Day of Resurrection had preceded, it was said: **﴿So today those who believed﴾**; and **(today)** is in the accusative governed by **(yaḍḥakūna)**, laughing at them in the Hereafter. **(observing)** is a circumstantial state of the pronoun in **(yaḍḥakūna)**, meaning they laugh while looking at them and at what they are in of humiliation and punishment after honor and bliss. Ka'b said to the people of Paradise: windows through which they look at the people of the Fire. It was also said: a transparent curtain between them through which they see their condition. **﴿Have they been rewarded?﴾**, that is, were they recompensed? It is said: **thawwaba** and **athāba** when one repays him. From it is the poet's saying:

*I will reward you, or a rewarder on my behalf will reward you, and it is enough for you that you be praised and thanked.*

This is an interrogative with the meaning of confirmation for the believers, meaning: were they recompensed for it? It was also said: **﴿Have they been rewarded?﴾** is attached to **(observing)**, and **(observing)** is governed by the sentence in a position of accusative after dropping the preposition **ilā** ("to"). The majority recited **﴿hal thuwwiba﴾** with the lām of **hal** pronounced clearly, while the two Naḥwīs (al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ) and Ḥamzah, and Ibn Muḥaysin, assimilated it into the thāʾ. In His words **﴿what they used to do﴾** there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: "a recompense or a punishment for what they used to do."

[p. 441] **﴿Those who deny﴾**: a description of blame. **﴿every transgressor﴾**: one who exceeds the limit. **(sinful)**: an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālagha). The majority of readers recited **(idhā)**, while al-Hasan recited **(a-idhā)**, with the hamzah of interrogation. The majority recited **(tutlā)** with the feminine tā', while Abu Ḥaywa and Ibn Miqsam recited it with yā'. It was said: this was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith. **﴿Nay, but rān﴾**: it was read with the lām of (bal) assimilated into the rā' (idghām), and also with the lām made clear (idhhār). Ḥamzah paused on (bal) with a light, brief pause to make the clarity of the idhhār evident. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Bādhish said: "The readers (qurrā') agreed on the assimilation of the lām into the rā', except for Ḥafṣ's pause on (bal), after which he says (rān)." In the book of Ibn 'Aṭiyya: "Nāfi' recited ﴿Nay, but rān﴾ without assimilation." And in it also: "Nāfi' also recited with assimilation and imāla." Sībawayh said: with a lām followed by a rā', as in (asfalu raḥimihi), both clarification (bayān) and assimilation (idghām) are good. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It was read with assimilation of the lām into the rā' and with clarification; the assimilation is better, and the alif was inclined (imāla) and emphasized (tafkhīm)." End of quotation. Sībawayh also said: when the lām is not the lām of definiteness, as the lām of (hal) and (bal), assimilation in some of them is better, such as (hal ra'ayta); if you do not assimilate and say (hal ra'ayta), it is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, which is rare but permissible. End of quotation.

Al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī said: it is sin upon sin. Al-Ḥasan said: until his heart dies. Al-Suddī said: until the heart turns black. A ḥadīth similar to this is also reported. Al-Kalbī said: He sealed (ṭaba'a) upon their hearts. Ibn Salām said: He covered them.

**﴿what they used to earn﴾**: Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: He attached the blame to them for what they earned, even though that occurs by creation and origination from Him, Exalted is He, because reward and punishment are tied to the servant's acquisition (kasb). The pronoun in His words **(innahum)** refers to the disbelievers. Whoever holds the view of seeing (Allah), which is the position of the People of the Sunnah, says that these will not see their Lord; they are veiled from Him. Mālik used this verse as evidence for the view of seeing by way of the indication of the discourse (dalīl al-khiṭāb), since if He veiled all, this specification would not be meaningful. Al-Shāfi'ī said: Since He veiled a people by displeasure, it indicates that another people will see Him with good pleasure. Whoever holds that there is no seeing, which is the position of the Mu'tazilah, says: they will be veiled from their Lord and His forgiveness. End of quotation. Anas ibn Mālik said: When He veiled His enemies so that they did not see Him, He manifested Himself to His friends until they saw Him. Al-Zamakhsharī said: **(kallā)** is a rebuke against the earning that has covered their hearts with rust, and their being veiled from Him is an image of contempt for them and of humiliating them, because kings grant access only to the notables who are honored in their sight, while only the lowly and despised are veiled from them. A poet said:

*When they approach the gate of a man of reproach, they are welcomed, while people are divided between one who is welcomed and one who is veiled.*

And from Ibn 'Abbās, Qatādah, and Ibn Abī Mulaykah: veiled from His mercy. And from Ibn Kaysān: from His honor. End of quotation. And from Mujāhid: the meaning is that they are veiled from His honor and His mercy. **(from their Lord)** is attached to **(veiled)**, and it is the governing element of **(yawma'idhin)**. Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: **﴿this which﴾**, meaning the sentence, is the object of an unspecified agent, because it is a saying in which the verb is constructed passively, namely (yuqālu). End of quotation. The discussion of the like of this was given earlier, at the beginning of al-Baqarah, in His words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11].

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿No! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾, ﴿And what will make you know what ʿIlliyyūn is?﴾, ﴿A written record﴾, ﴿witnessed by those brought near﴾, ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾, ﴿They are given to drink from a sealed wine﴾, ﴿its seal is musk﴾, ﴿and for that let the competitors compete﴾, ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnīm﴾, ﴿a spring from which those brought near drink﴾, ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾, ﴿and when they passed by them, they would wink at one another﴾, ﴿and when they returned to their people, they returned jesting﴾, ﴿and when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are astray"﴾, ﴿but they were not sent as guardians over them﴾, ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do?﴾.

Abu al-Fatḥ said: its proper form should be ʿIlliyyah, as they say of an upper room ʿilliyyah; when the tā' was deleted they compensated for it with the plural suffix of the masculine sound plural, the wāw and nūn. It was also said: it is an attribute of the angels, and therefore it takes the wāw and nūn plural. Al-Farrā' said: it is a noun established in the form of a plural, having no singular from its own form, like ʿishrīn and thalāthīn; when the Arabs form a plural and it has no pattern from its singular or dual, they use the wāw and nūn for both masculine and feminine. Al-Zajjāj said: this noun is inflected like the plural: "hadhihi Qansarūn, wa ra'aytu Qansarīn." **(ʿIlliyyūn)** is: the angels, or the lofty places, or a proper name for the register of good in which is recorded all that the angels and the righteous of the two species (jinn and mankind) know; or it is "highness upon doubled highness." Three opinions are from al-Zamakhsharī.

Abū Muslim said: **﴿the record of the righteous﴾** means the writing of their deeds, **﴿is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾**. Then He described ʿIlliyyūn as **"a written record"** in which are all the deeds of the righteous. As for it being a place, they differed about its specification in a confused manner, and we have turned away from mentioning it. The grammatical analysis of **﴿is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾** and **﴿a written record﴾** is like that of **﴿is in Sijjīn﴾** [al-Muṭaffifīn: 7] and **﴿a written record﴾**. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: **﴿a written record﴾** in this verse is the predicate of **inna**, and the adverbial phrase is cancelled. End of quotation. This is what he said regarding **﴿is in Sijjīn﴾** [al-Muṭaffifīn: 7], and we have already refuted him on that, and this is similar to it. **(Those brought near)** here, Ibn ʿAbbās and others said, are the angels, the people of each heaven. **(observing)**: Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, and Mujāhid said: they observe what has been prepared for them of honors. Muqātil said: they observe the people of the Fire. It was said: some of them look at others.

The majority recited **(taʿrifu)** with the feminine tā' of address, addressed either to the Messenger or to the one who looks; **﴿the radiance of bliss﴾** is in the accusative. Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Ṭalḥah, Shaybah, Yaʿqūb, and al-Zaʿfarānī recited **(tuʿrafu)** in the passive voice, with **(radiance)** in the nominative. Zayd ibn ʿAlī also recited likewise, except that he recited **(yuʿrafu)** with yā', since the feminine marking of **naḍrah** is metaphorical. The meaning of **al-naḍrah** has been explained earlier in His words: ﴿radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insān: 11].

Abū ʿAlī said: that is, its spices, which are cut up, and the sharpness of the fragrance together with the goodness of the taste. It was said: it is mixed with camphor and its mixture is sealed with musk. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: al-khitām is the clay with which something is sealed. Likewise Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: its vessel was sealed with musk instead of clay. A poet said:

*As if a clear-sparkling wine from Buṣrā, whose scent was carried by the breezes, were tightly sealed.*

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿No! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾, ﴿And what will make you know what ʿIlliyyūn is?﴾, ﴿A written record﴾, ﴿witnessed by those brought near﴾, ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾, ﴿They are given to drink from a sealed wine﴾, ﴿its seal is musk﴾, ﴿and for that let the competitors compete﴾, ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnīm﴾, ﴿a spring from which those brought near drink﴾, ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾, ﴿and when they passed by them, they would wink at one another﴾, ﴿and when they returned to their people, they returned jesting﴾, ﴿and when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are astray"﴾, ﴿but they were not sent as guardians over them﴾, ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do?﴾.

[p. 442] When He, Exalted is He, mentioned the matter of the book of the wicked, He followed it with the mention of the book of their opposites, so that the difference would be made clear. **(ʿIlliyyūn)**: a plural whose singular is ʿAliyy, derived from **al-ʿUluww** (height), and it is an intensive form; this was said by Yūnus and Ibn Jinnī. Abu al-Fatḥ said: its proper form should be ʿIlliyyah, as they say of an upper room ʿilliyyah; when the tā' was deleted they compensated for it with the plural suffix of the masculine sound plural, the wāw and nūn. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: **﴿a written record﴾** in this verse is the predicate of **inna**, and the adverbial phrase is cancelled. End of quotation. This is what he said regarding **﴿is in Sijjīn﴾** [al-Muṭaffifīn: 7], and we have already refuted him on that, and this is similar to it. **(Those brought near)** here, Ibn ʿAbbās and others said, are the angels, the people of each heaven. **(observing)**: Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, and Mujāhid said: they observe what has been prepared for them of honors. Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Ṭalḥah, Shaybah, Yaʿqūb, and al-Zaʿfarānī recited **(tuʿrafu)** in the passive voice, with **(radiance)** in the nominative. Zayd ibn ʿAlī also recited likewise, except that he recited **(yuʿrafu)** with yā', since the feminine marking of **naḍrah** is metaphorical. The meaning of **al-naḍrah** has been explained earlier in His words: ﴿radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insān: 11].

These disbelievers of Makkah are said to be: Abū Jahl, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, and al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil. The believers are: ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb, Khabbāb, Bilāl, and others of the poor believers. It was said: this was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith. **﴿Nay, but rān﴾**: it was read with the lām of (bal) assimilated into the rā' (idghām), and also with the lām made clear (idhhār). Ḥamzah paused on (bal) with a light, brief pause to make the clarity of the idhhār evident. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Bādhish said: "The readers (qurrā') agreed on the assimilation of the lām into the rā', except for Ḥafṣ's pause on (bal), after which he says (rān)." What he mentioned as a consensus is not as he stated, for in the book al-Lawāmiḥ, from Qālūn through all his transmission routes, the lām is made clear before the rā', as in His words: ﴿Nay, but Allah raised him up to Himself﴾ [al-Nisā': 158], and ﴿Nay, but your Lord﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 56]. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It was read with assimilation of the lām into the rā' and with clarification; the assimilation is better, and the alif was inclined (imāla) and emphasized (tafkhīm)." End of quotation. Sībawayh also said: when the lām is not the lām of definiteness, as the lām of (hal) and (bal), assimilation in some of them is better, such as (hal ra'ayta); if you do not assimilate and say (hal ra'ayta), it is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, which is rare but permissible. Al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī said: it is sin upon sin. Al-Ḥasan said: until his heart dies. Al-Suddī said: until the heart turns black. A ḥadīth similar to this is also reported. Al-Kalbī said: He sealed (ṭaba'a) upon their hearts. Ibn Salām said: He covered them.

**﴿what they used to earn﴾**: Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: He attached the blame to them for what they earned, even though that occurs by creation and origination from Him, Exalted is He, because reward and punishment are tied to the servant's acquisition (kasb). The pronoun in His words **(innahum)** refers to the disbelievers. Whoever holds the view of seeing (Allah), which is the position of the People of the Sunnah, says that these will not see their Lord; they are veiled from Him. Al-Shāfi'ī said: Since He veiled a people by displeasure, it indicates that another people will see Him with good pleasure. Whoever holds that there is no seeing, which is the position of the Mu'tazilah, says: they will be veiled from their Lord and His forgiveness. End of quotation. Anas ibn Mālik said: When He veiled His enemies so that they did not see Him, He manifested Himself to His friends until they saw Him. Al-Zamakhsharī said: **(kallā)** is a rebuke against the earning that has covered their hearts with rust, and their being veiled from Him is an image of contempt for them and of humiliating them, because kings grant access only to the notables who are honored in their sight, while only the lowly and despised are veiled from them. *When they approach the gate of a man of reproach, they are welcomed, while people are divided between one who is welcomed and one who is veiled.*

The majority recited **(tutlā)** with the feminine tā', while Abu Ḥaywa and Ibn Miqsam recited it with yā'. It was said: this was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith. **﴿Nay, but rān﴾**: it was read with the lām of (bal) assimilated into the rā' (idghām), and also with the lām made clear (idhhār). Ḥamzah paused on (bal) with a light, brief pause to make the clarity of the idhhār evident. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Bādhish said: "The readers (qurrā') agreed on the assimilation of the lām into the rā', except for Ḥafṣ's pause on (bal), after which he says (rān)." In the book of Ibn 'Aṭiyya: "Nāfi' recited ﴿Nay, but rān﴾ without assimilation." And in it also: "Nāfi' also recited with assimilation and imāla." Sībawayh said: with a lām followed by a rā', as in (asfalu raḥimihi), both clarification (bayān) and assimilation (idghām) are good. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It was read with assimilation of the lām into the rā' and with clarification; the assimilation is better, and the alif was inclined (imāla) and emphasized (tafkhīm)." End of quotation. Sībawayh also said: when the lām is not the lām of definiteness, as the lām of (hal) and (bal), assimilation in some of them is better, such as (hal ra'ayta); if you do not assimilate and say (hal ra'ayta), it is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, which is rare but permissible. End of quotation.

Al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī said: it is sin upon sin. Al-Ḥasan said: until his heart dies. Al-Suddī said: until the heart turns black. A ḥadīth similar to this is also reported. Al-Kalbī said: He sealed (ṭaba'a) upon their hearts. Ibn Salām said: He covered them.

**﴿what they used to earn﴾**: Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: He attached the blame to them for what they earned, even though that occurs by creation and origination from Him, Exalted is He, because reward and punishment are tied to the servant's acquisition (kasb). The pronoun in His words **(innahum)** refers to the disbelievers. Whoever holds the view of seeing (Allah), which is the position of the People of the Sunnah, says that these will not see their Lord; they are veiled from Him. Mālik used this verse as evidence for the view of seeing by way of the indication of the discourse (dalīl al-khiṭāb), since if He veiled all, this specification would not be meaningful. Al-Shāfi'ī said: Since He veiled a people by displeasure, it indicates that another people will see Him with good pleasure. Whoever holds that there is no seeing, which is the position of the Mu'tazilah, says: they will be veiled from their Lord and His forgiveness. End of quotation. Anas ibn Mālik said: When He veiled His enemies so that they did not see Him, He manifested Himself to His friends until they saw Him. A poet said:

*When they approach the gate of a man of reproach, they are welcomed, while people are divided between one who is welcomed and one who is veiled.*

And from Ibn 'Abbās, Qatādah, and Ibn Abī Mulaykah: veiled from His mercy. And from Ibn Kaysān: from His honor. End of quotation. And from Mujāhid: the meaning is that they are veiled from His honor and His mercy. **(from their Lord)** is attached to **(veiled)**, and it is the governing element of **(yawma'idhin)**. Then, together with being veiled from Allah, they are the burners of the Fire, and this is the fruit of the veil. **﴿Then it will be said﴾**, that is, the keepers of the Fire will say to them: **(this)**, that is, the punishment and the burning of the Fire, and this is **﴿the Day which you used to deny﴾**. His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿No! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾, ﴿And what will make you know what ʿIlliyyūn is?﴾, ﴿A written record﴾, ﴿witnessed by those brought near﴾, ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾, ﴿They are given to drink from a sealed wine﴾, ﴿its seal is musk﴾, ﴿and for that let the competitors compete﴾, ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnīm﴾, ﴿a spring from which those brought near drink﴾, ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾, ﴿and when they passed by them, they would wink at one another﴾, ﴿and when they returned to their people, they returned jesting﴾, ﴿and when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are astray"﴾, ﴿but they were not sent as guardians over them﴾, ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do?﴾.

Al-Farrā' said: it is a noun established in the form of a plural, having no singular from its own form, like ʿishrīn and thalāthīn; when the Arabs form a plural and it has no pattern from its singular or dual, they use the wāw and nūn for both masculine and feminine. Muqātil said: they observe the people of the Fire. It was said: some of them look at others.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī also recited likewise, except that he recited **(yuʿrafu)** with yā', since the feminine marking of **naḍrah** is metaphorical. The meaning of **al-naḍrah** has been explained earlier in His words: ﴿radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insān: 11].

It was said: it is mixed with camphor and its mixture is sealed with musk. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: al-khitām is the clay with which something is sealed. Likewise Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: its vessel was sealed with musk instead of clay. A poet said:

*As if a clear-sparkling wine from Buṣrā, whose scent was carried by the breezes, were tightly sealed.*

[p. 443] The position of the majority is that the righteous are the companions of the right hand, and that those brought near are the foremost. Some people said: the righteous and those brought near in this verse have one meaning, applying to everyone who is given bliss in Paradise.

It is reported that ʿAlī and a group of believers with him passed by a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh, and they laughed at them and mocked them in play. Then the verse was revealed: **﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes﴾**, before ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, reached the Messenger (ﷺ). Abū Rajāʾ, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, Abū Jaʿfar, and Ḥafṣ recited it without alif. The pronoun in the nominative in **(raʾawhum)** refers to the guilty, meaning: when they saw the believers, they attributed them to error, and they were right in attributing it to them.

It was also said: a transparent curtain between them through which they see their condition. **﴿Have they been rewarded?﴾**, that is, were they recompensed? It is said: **thawwaba** and **athāba** when one repays him. From it is the poet's saying:

*I will reward you, or a rewarder on my behalf will reward you, and it is enough for you that you be praised and thanked.*

This is an interrogative with the meaning of confirmation for the believers, meaning: were they recompensed for it? It was also said: **﴿Have they been rewarded?﴾** is attached to **(observing)**, and **(observing)** is governed by the sentence in a position of accusative after dropping the preposition **ilā** ("to"). From al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿĪsā, and Aḥmad ibn Jubayr al-Anṭākī, from al-Kisāʾī: a kasrah on the tā', meaning its last, like His words: ﴿and the Seal of the Prophets﴾. There is an ellipsis in it, meaning: the seal of its fragrance is musk, or its seal with which it is sealed and cut off.

**﴿from Tasnīm﴾**: ʿAbd Allāh and Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is the most noble drink of Paradise, and it is a masculine noun for the water of a spring in Paradise. Al-Zamakhsharī said: **(Tasnīm)** is a proper name for a specific spring, named Tasnīm, which is the verbal noun of sannamahu, meaning "he raised it." **(ʿAynan)** is in the accusative as an expression of praise. Al-Zajjāj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). End of quotation. Al-Akhfash said: they are given to drink a spring (ʿaynan) **﴿from which they drink﴾**, meaning they drink it, or from it; or the verb **(yashrabu)** is implicitly made to mean **(yurwā)**, and about **(bihā)** there are several views. **(those brought near)**: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and Abū Ṣāliḥ said: those brought near drink it pure, and it is mixed for the righteous. [p. 443] The position of the majority is that the righteous are the companions of the right hand, and that those brought near are the foremost. Some people said: the righteous and those brought near in this verse have one meaning, applying to everyone who is given bliss in Paradise.

It is reported that ʿAlī and a group of believers with him passed by a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh, and they laughed at them and mocked them in play. Then the verse was revealed: **﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes﴾**, before ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, reached the Messenger (ﷺ). These disbelievers of Makkah are said to be: Abū Jahl, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, and al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil. The believers are: ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb, Khabbāb, Bilāl, and others of the poor believers. The apparent view is that the pronoun in **(marrū)** refers to **﴿those who committed crimes﴾**, since in that there is consistency of pronouns for one referent. It was also said: it refers to the believers, meaning: when the believers passed by the disbelievers, the disbelievers would wink, that is, indicate with their eyes. **(jesting)**: that is, delighting in mentioning them and in laughing at them. The majority recited **(fākihīn)** with an alif, meaning possessors of jest, play, and joy at their mockery of the people of faith. Abū Rajāʾ, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, Abū Jaʿfar, and Ḥafṣ recited it without alif. The pronoun in the nominative in **(raʾawhum)** refers to the guilty, meaning: when they saw the believers, they attributed them to error, and they were right in attributing it to them.

**﴿but they were not sent﴾** as guardians over the disbelievers. The mention of their being astray is a provocation of speech among them, and there was in the verse some gentleness (muwādaʿah), meaning: the believers were not sent to be guardians over the disbelievers. This is according to the view that this was abrogated by the verse of the sword. Al-Zamakhsharī said: and they were not sent as guardians over them, as a denial of their hindering them from polytheism and of their calling them to Islam and their striving in that. Since the mention of the Day of Resurrection had preceded, it was said: **﴿So today those who believed﴾**; and **(today)** is in the accusative governed by **(yaḍḥakūna)**, laughing at them in the Hereafter. **(observing)** is a circumstantial state of the pronoun in **(yaḍḥakūna)**, meaning they laugh while looking at them and at what they are in of humiliation and punishment after honor and bliss. Ka'b said to the people of Paradise: windows through which they look at the people of the Fire. It was also said: a transparent curtain between them through which they see their condition. **﴿Have they been rewarded?﴾**, that is, were they recompensed? It is said: **thawwaba** and **athāba** when one repays him. From it is the poet's saying:

*I will reward you, or a rewarder on my behalf will reward you, and it is enough for you that you be praised and thanked.*

This is an interrogative with the meaning of confirmation for the believers, meaning: were they recompensed for it? It was also said: **﴿Have they been rewarded?﴾** is attached to **(observing)**, and **(observing)** is governed by the sentence in a position of accusative after dropping the preposition **ilā** ("to"). The majority recited **﴿hal thuwwiba﴾** with the lām of **hal** pronounced clearly, while the two Naḥwīs (al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ) and Ḥamzah, and Ibn Muḥaysin, assimilated it into the thāʾ. In His words **﴿what they used to do﴾** there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: "a recompense or a punishment for what they used to do."

[p. 441] **﴿Those who deny﴾**: a description of blame. **﴿every transgressor﴾**: one who exceeds the limit. **(sinful)**: an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālagha). The majority of readers recited **(idhā)**, while al-Hasan recited **(a-idhā)**, with the hamzah of interrogation. The majority recited **(tutlā)** with the feminine tā', while Abu Ḥaywa and Ibn Miqsam recited it with yā'. It was said: this was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith. **﴿Nay, but rān﴾**: it was read with the lām of (bal) assimilated into the rā' (idghām), and also with the lām made clear (idhhār). Ḥamzah paused on (bal) with a light, brief pause to make the clarity of the idhhār evident. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Bādhish said: "The readers (qurrā') agreed on the assimilation of the lām into the rā', except for Ḥafṣ's pause on (bal), after which he says (rān)." In the book of Ibn 'Aṭiyya: "Nāfi' recited ﴿Nay, but rān﴾ without assimilation." And in it also: "Nāfi' also recited with assimilation and imāla." Sībawayh said: with a lām followed by a rā', as in (asfalu raḥimihi), both clarification (bayān) and assimilation (idghām) are good. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It was read with assimilation of the lām into the rā' and with clarification; the assimilation is better, and the alif was inclined (imāla) and emphasized (tafkhīm)." End of quotation. Sībawayh also said: when the lām is not the lām of definiteness, as the lām of (hal) and (bal), assimilation in some of them is better, such as (hal ra'ayta); if you do not assimilate and say (hal ra'ayta), it is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, which is rare but permissible. End of quotation.

Al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī said: it is sin upon sin. Al-Ḥasan said: until his heart dies. Al-Suddī said: until the heart turns black. A ḥadīth similar to this is also reported. Al-Kalbī said: He sealed (ṭaba'a) upon their hearts. Ibn Salām said: He covered them.

**﴿what they used to earn﴾**: Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: He attached the blame to them for what they earned, even though that occurs by creation and origination from Him, Exalted is He, because reward and punishment are tied to the servant's acquisition (kasb). The pronoun in His words **(innahum)** refers to the disbelievers. Whoever holds the view of seeing (Allah), which is the position of the People of the Sunnah, says that these will not see their Lord; they are veiled from Him. Mālik used this verse as evidence for the view of seeing by way of the indication of the discourse (dalīl al-khiṭāb), since if He veiled all, this specification would not be meaningful. Al-Shāfi'ī said: Since He veiled a people by displeasure, it indicates that another people will see Him with good pleasure. Whoever holds that there is no seeing, which is the position of the Mu'tazilah, says: they will be veiled from their Lord and His forgiveness. End of quotation. Anas ibn Mālik said: When He veiled His enemies so that they did not see Him, He manifested Himself to His friends until they saw Him. Al-Zamakhsharī said: **(kallā)** is a rebuke against the earning that has covered their hearts with rust, and their being veiled from Him is an image of contempt for them and of humiliating them, because kings grant access only to the notables who are honored in their sight, while only the lowly and despised are veiled from them. A poet said:

*When they approach the gate of a man of reproach, they are welcomed, while people are divided between one who is welcomed and one who is veiled.*

And from Ibn 'Abbās, Qatādah, and Ibn Abī Mulaykah: veiled from His mercy. And from Ibn Kaysān: from His honor. End of quotation. And from Mujāhid: the meaning is that they are veiled from His honor and His mercy. **(from their Lord)** is attached to **(veiled)**, and it is the governing element of **(yawma'idhin)**. Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: **﴿this which﴾**, meaning the sentence, is the object of an unspecified agent, because it is a saying in which the verb is constructed passively, namely (yuqālu). End of quotation. The discussion of the like of this was given earlier, at the beginning of al-Baqarah, in His words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11].

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿No! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾, ﴿And what will make you know what ʿIlliyyūn is?﴾, ﴿A written record﴾, ﴿witnessed by those brought near﴾, ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾, ﴿They are given to drink from a sealed wine﴾, ﴿its seal is musk﴾, ﴿and for that let the competitors compete﴾, ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnīm﴾, ﴿a spring from which those brought near drink﴾, ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾, ﴿and when they passed by them, they would wink at one another﴾, ﴿and when they returned to their people, they returned jesting﴾, ﴿and when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are astray"﴾, ﴿but they were not sent as guardians over them﴾, ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do?﴾.

Abu al-Fatḥ said: its proper form should be ʿIlliyyah, as they say of an upper room ʿilliyyah; when the tā' was deleted they compensated for it with the plural suffix of the masculine sound plural, the wāw and nūn. It was also said: it is an attribute of the angels, and therefore it takes the wāw and nūn plural. Al-Farrā' said: it is a noun established in the form of a plural, having no singular from its own form, like ʿishrīn and thalāthīn; when the Arabs form a plural and it has no pattern from its singular or dual, they use the wāw and nūn for both masculine and feminine. Al-Zajjāj said: this noun is inflected like the plural: "hadhihi Qansarūn, wa ra'aytu Qansarīn." **(ʿIlliyyūn)** is: the angels, or the lofty places, or a proper name for the register of good in which is recorded all that the angels and the righteous of the two species (jinn and mankind) know; or it is "highness upon doubled highness." Three opinions are from al-Zamakhsharī.

Abū Muslim said: **﴿the record of the righteous﴾** means the writing of their deeds, **﴿is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾**. Then He described ʿIlliyyūn as **"a written record"** in which are all the deeds of the righteous. As for it being a place, they differed about its specification in a confused manner, and we have turned away from mentioning it. The grammatical analysis of **﴿is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾** and **﴿a written record﴾** is like that of **﴿is in Sijjīn﴾** [al-Muṭaffifīn: 7] and **﴿a written record﴾**. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: **﴿a written record﴾** in this verse is the predicate of **inna**, and the adverbial phrase is cancelled. End of quotation. This is what he said regarding **﴿is in Sijjīn﴾** [al-Muṭaffifīn: 7], and we have already refuted him on that, and this is similar to it. **(Those brought near)** here, Ibn ʿAbbās and others said, are the angels, the people of each heaven. **(observing)**: Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, and Mujāhid said: they observe what has been prepared for them of honors. Muqātil said: they observe the people of the Fire. It was said: some of them look at others.

The majority recited **(taʿrifu)** with the feminine tā' of address, addressed either to the Messenger or to the one who looks; **﴿the radiance of bliss﴾** is in the accusative. Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Ṭalḥah, Shaybah, Yaʿqūb, and al-Zaʿfarānī recited **(tuʿrafu)** in the passive voice, with **(radiance)** in the nominative. Zayd ibn ʿAlī also recited likewise, except that he recited **(yuʿrafu)** with yā', since the feminine marking of **naḍrah** is metaphorical. The meaning of **al-naḍrah** has been explained earlier in His words: ﴿radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insān: 11].

Abū ʿAlī said: that is, its spices, which are cut up, and the sharpness of the fragrance together with the goodness of the taste. It was said: it is mixed with camphor and its mixture is sealed with musk. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: al-khitām is the clay with which something is sealed. Likewise Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: its vessel was sealed with musk instead of clay. A poet said:

*As if a clear-sparkling wine from Buṣrā, whose scent was carried by the breezes, were tightly sealed.*

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿No! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾, ﴿And what will make you know what ʿIlliyyūn is?﴾, ﴿A written record﴾, ﴿witnessed by those brought near﴾, ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾, ﴿They are given to drink from a sealed wine﴾, ﴿its seal is musk﴾, ﴿and for that let the competitors compete﴾, ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnīm﴾, ﴿a spring from which those brought near drink﴾, ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾, ﴿and when they passed by them, they would wink at one another﴾, ﴿and when they returned to their people, they returned jesting﴾, ﴿and when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are astray"﴾, ﴿but they were not sent as guardians over them﴾, ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do?﴾.

[p. 442] When He, Exalted is He, mentioned the matter of the book of the wicked, He followed it with the mention of the book of their opposites, so that the difference would be made clear. **(ʿIlliyyūn)**: a plural whose singular is ʿAliyy, derived from **al-ʿUluww** (height), and it is an intensive form; this was said by Yūnus and Ibn Jinnī. Abu al-Fatḥ said: its proper form should be ʿIlliyyah, as they say of an upper room ʿilliyyah; when the tā' was deleted they compensated for it with the plural suffix of the masculine sound plural, the wāw and nūn. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: **﴿a written record﴾** in this verse is the predicate of **inna**, and the adverbial phrase is cancelled. End of quotation. This is what he said regarding **﴿is in Sijjīn﴾** [al-Muṭaffifīn: 7], and we have already refuted him on that, and this is similar to it. **(Those brought near)** here, Ibn ʿAbbās and others said, are the angels, the people of each heaven. **(observing)**: Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, and Mujāhid said: they observe what has been prepared for them of honors. Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Ṭalḥah, Shaybah, Yaʿqūb, and al-Zaʿfarānī recited **(tuʿrafu)** in the passive voice, with **(radiance)** in the nominative. Zayd ibn ʿAlī also recited likewise, except that he recited **(yuʿrafu)** with yā', since the feminine marking of **naḍrah** is metaphorical. The meaning of **al-naḍrah** has been explained earlier in His words: ﴿radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insān: 11].

These disbelievers of Makkah are said to be: Abū Jahl, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, and al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil. The believers are: ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb, Khabbāb, Bilāl, and others of the poor believers. It was said: this was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith. **﴿Nay, but rān﴾**: it was read with the lām of (bal) assimilated into the rā' (idghām), and also with the lām made clear (idhhār). Ḥamzah paused on (bal) with a light, brief pause to make the clarity of the idhhār evident. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Bādhish said: "The readers (qurrā') agreed on the assimilation of the lām into the rā', except for Ḥafṣ's pause on (bal), after which he says (rān)." What he mentioned as a consensus is not as he stated, for in the book al-Lawāmiḥ, from Qālūn through all his transmission routes, the lām is made clear before the rā', as in His words: ﴿Nay, but Allah raised him up to Himself﴾ [al-Nisā': 158], and ﴿Nay, but your Lord﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 56]. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It was read with assimilation of the lām into the rā' and with clarification; the assimilation is better, and the alif was inclined (imāla) and emphasized (tafkhīm)." End of quotation. Sībawayh also said: when the lām is not the lām of definiteness, as the lām of (hal) and (bal), assimilation in some of them is better, such as (hal ra'ayta); if you do not assimilate and say (hal ra'ayta), it is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, which is rare but permissible. Al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī said: it is sin upon sin. Al-Ḥasan said: until his heart dies. Al-Suddī said: until the heart turns black. A ḥadīth similar to this is also reported. Al-Kalbī said: He sealed (ṭaba'a) upon their hearts. Ibn Salām said: He covered them.

**﴿what they used to earn﴾**: Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: He attached the blame to them for what they earned, even though that occurs by creation and origination from Him, Exalted is He, because reward and punishment are tied to the servant's acquisition (kasb). The pronoun in His words **(innahum)** refers to the disbelievers. Whoever holds the view of seeing (Allah), which is the position of the People of the Sunnah, says that these will not see their Lord; they are veiled from Him. Al-Shāfi'ī said: Since He veiled a people by displeasure, it indicates that another people will see Him with good pleasure. Whoever holds that there is no seeing, which is the position of the Mu'tazilah, says: they will be veiled from their Lord and His forgiveness. End of quotation. Anas ibn Mālik said: When He veiled His enemies so that they did not see Him, He manifested Himself to His friends until they saw Him. Al-Zamakhsharī said: **(kallā)** is a rebuke against the earning that has covered their hearts with rust, and their being veiled from Him is an image of contempt for them and of humiliating them, because kings grant access only to the notables who are honored in their sight, while only the lowly and despised are veiled from them. *When they approach the gate of a man of reproach, they are welcomed, while people are divided between one who is welcomed and one who is veiled.*

[p. 441] **﴿Those who deny﴾**: a description of blame. **﴿every transgressor﴾**: one who exceeds the limit. **(sinful)**: an intensive form (ṣīghat mubālagha). The majority of readers recited **(idhā)**, while al-Hasan recited **(a-idhā)**, with the hamzah of interrogation. The majority recited **(tutlā)** with the feminine tā', while Abu Ḥaywa and Ibn Miqsam recited it with yā'. It was said: this was revealed concerning al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith. **﴿Nay, but rān﴾**: it was read with the lām of (bal) assimilated into the rā' (idghām), and also with the lām made clear (idhhār). Ḥamzah paused on (bal) with a light, brief pause to make the clarity of the idhhār evident. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Bādhish said: "The readers (qurrā') agreed on the assimilation of the lām into the rā', except for Ḥafṣ's pause on (bal), after which he says (rān)." What he mentioned as a consensus is not as he stated, for in the book al-Lawāmiḥ, from Qālūn through all his transmission routes, the lām is made clear before the rā', as in His words: ﴿Nay, but Allah raised him up to Himself﴾ [al-Nisā': 158], and ﴿Nay, but your Lord﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 56]. In the book of Ibn 'Aṭiyya: "Nāfi' recited ﴿Nay, but rān﴾ without assimilation." And in it also: "Nāfi' also recited with assimilation and imāla." Sībawayh said: with a lām followed by a rā', as in (asfalu raḥimihi), both clarification (bayān) and assimilation (idghām) are good. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It was read with assimilation of the lām into the rā' and with clarification; the assimilation is better, and the alif was inclined (imāla) and emphasized (tafkhīm)." End of quotation. Sībawayh also said: when the lām is not the lām of definiteness, as the lām of (hal) and (bal), assimilation in some of them is better, such as (hal ra'ayta); if you do not assimilate and say (hal ra'ayta), it is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz, which is rare but permissible. End of quotation.

Al-Ḥasan and al-Suddī said: it is sin upon sin. Al-Ḥasan said: until his heart dies. Al-Suddī said: until the heart turns black. A ḥadīth similar to this is also reported. Al-Kalbī said: He sealed (ṭaba'a) upon their hearts. Ibn Salām said: He covered them.

**﴿what they used to earn﴾**: Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: He attached the blame to them for what they earned, even though that occurs by creation and origination from Him, Exalted is He, because reward and punishment are tied to the servant's acquisition (kasb). The pronoun in His words **(innahum)** refers to the disbelievers. Whoever holds the view of seeing (Allah), which is the position of the People of the Sunnah, says that these will not see their Lord; they are veiled from Him. Mālik used this verse as evidence for the view of seeing by way of the indication of the discourse (dalīl al-khiṭāb), since if He veiled all, this specification would not be meaningful. Al-Shāfi'ī said: Since He veiled a people by displeasure, it indicates that another people will see Him with good pleasure. Whoever holds that there is no seeing, which is the position of the Mu'tazilah, says: they will be veiled from their Lord and His forgiveness. End of quotation. Anas ibn Mālik said: When He veiled His enemies so that they did not see Him, He manifested Himself to His friends until they saw Him. Al-Zamakhsharī said: **(kallā)** is a rebuke against the earning that has covered their hearts with rust, and their being veiled from Him is an image of contempt for them and of humiliating them, because kings grant access only to the notables who are honored in their sight, while only the lowly and despised are veiled from them. A poet said:

*When they approach the gate of a man of reproach, they are welcomed, while people are divided between one who is welcomed and one who is veiled.*

And from Ibn 'Abbās, Qatādah, and Ibn Abī Mulaykah: veiled from His mercy. And from Ibn Kaysān: from His honor. End of quotation. And from Mujāhid: the meaning is that they are veiled from His honor and His mercy. **(from their Lord)** is attached to **(veiled)**, and it is the governing element of **(yawma'idhin)**. The tanwīn is the tanwīn of substitution (ʿiwaḍ) for a deleted sentence, and no near sentence preceded to serve as its substitute, but ﴿the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Muṭaffifīn: 6] preceded, so it is the substitute for this sentence, as if it were said: "the day when mankind stands." Then, together with being veiled from Allah, they are the burners of the Fire, and this is the fruit of the veil. **﴿Then it will be said﴾**, that is, the keepers of the Fire will say to them: **(this)**, that is, the punishment and the burning of the Fire, and this is **﴿the Day which you used to deny﴾**. Ibn 'Aṭiyya said: **﴿this which﴾**, meaning the sentence, is the object of an unspecified agent, because it is a saying in which the verb is constructed passively, namely (yuqālu). End of quotation. The discussion of the like of this was given earlier, at the beginning of al-Baqarah, in His words: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 11].

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿No! Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾, ﴿And what will make you know what ʿIlliyyūn is?﴾, ﴿A written record﴾, ﴿witnessed by those brought near﴾, ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿You will recognize in their faces the radiance of bliss﴾, ﴿They are given to drink from a sealed wine﴾, ﴿its seal is musk﴾, ﴿and for that let the competitors compete﴾, ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnīm﴾, ﴿a spring from which those brought near drink﴾, ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾, ﴿and when they passed by them, they would wink at one another﴾, ﴿and when they returned to their people, they returned jesting﴾, ﴿and when they saw them, they said, "Indeed, these are astray"﴾, ﴿but they were not sent as guardians over them﴾, ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, ﴿on couches, observing﴾, ﴿Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do?﴾.

[p. 442] When He, Exalted is He, mentioned the matter of the book of the wicked, He followed it with the mention of the book of their opposites, so that the difference would be made clear. **(ʿIlliyyūn)**: a plural whose singular is ʿAliyy, derived from **al-ʿUluww** (height), and it is an intensive form; this was said by Yūnus and Ibn Jinnī. Abu al-Fatḥ said: its proper form should be ʿIlliyyah, as they say of an upper room ʿilliyyah; when the tā' was deleted they compensated for it with the plural suffix of the masculine sound plural, the wāw and nūn. It was also said: it is an attribute of the angels, and therefore it takes the wāw and nūn plural. Al-Farrā' said: it is a noun established in the form of a plural, having no singular from its own form, like ʿishrīn and thalāthīn; when the Arabs form a plural and it has no pattern from its singular or dual, they use the wāw and nūn for both masculine and feminine. Al-Zajjāj said: this noun is inflected like the plural: "hadhihi Qansarūn, wa ra'aytu Qansarīn." **(ʿIlliyyūn)** is: the angels, or the lofty places, or a proper name for the register of good in which is recorded all that the angels and the righteous of the two species (jinn and mankind) know; or it is "highness upon doubled highness." Three opinions are from al-Zamakhsharī.

Abū Muslim said: **﴿the record of the righteous﴾** means the writing of their deeds, **﴿is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾**. Then He described ʿIlliyyūn as **"a written record"** in which are all the deeds of the righteous. As for it being a place, they differed about its specification in a confused manner, and we have turned away from mentioning it. The grammatical analysis of **﴿is in ʿIlliyyūn﴾** and **﴿a written record﴾** is like that of **﴿is in Sijjīn﴾** [al-Muṭaffifīn: 7] and **﴿a written record﴾**. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: **﴿a written record﴾** in this verse is the predicate of **inna**, and the adverbial phrase is cancelled. End of quotation. This is what he said regarding **﴿is in Sijjīn﴾** [al-Muṭaffifīn: 7], and we have already refuted him on that, and this is similar to it. **(Those brought near)** here, Ibn ʿAbbās and others said, are the angels, the people of each heaven. **(observing)**: Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, and Mujāhid said: they observe what has been prepared for them of honors. Muqātil said: they observe the people of the Fire. It was said: some of them look at others.

The majority recited **(taʿrifu)** with the feminine tā' of address, addressed either to the Messenger or to the one who looks; **﴿the radiance of bliss﴾** is in the accusative. Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Ṭalḥah, Shaybah, Yaʿqūb, and al-Zaʿfarānī recited **(tuʿrafu)** in the passive voice, with **(radiance)** in the nominative. Zayd ibn ʿAlī also recited likewise, except that he recited **(yuʿrafu)** with yā', since the feminine marking of **naḍrah** is metaphorical. The meaning of **al-naḍrah** has been explained earlier in His words: ﴿radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insān: 11].

**(sealed)**: Apparently the wine was sealed, meaning it was perfumed and cleansed with a musk-like scent, as what follows it explains. It was also said: its vessels, of cups and jugs, are sealed with musk in place of clay. The majority recited **(khitāmuhu)**, meaning its mixture and blend; this was said by ʿAbd Allāh and ʿAlqamah. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Ḥasan said: its meaning is its final part (khātimatuhu), that is, one finds at the end of the drink the scent of musk. Abū ʿAlī said: that is, its spices, which are cut up, and the sharpness of the fragrance together with the goodness of the taste. It was said: it is mixed with camphor and its mixture is sealed with musk. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: al-khitām is the clay with which something is sealed. Likewise Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: its vessel was sealed with musk instead of clay. A poet said:

*As if a clear-sparkling wine from Buṣrā, whose scent was carried by the breezes, were tightly sealed.*

ʿAlī, al-Nakhaʿī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Abū Ḥaywa, Ibn Abī ʿAblah, and al-Kisāʾī recited **(khātamuhu)** with an alif after the khāʾ and a fatḥah on the tā'. This is a clear meaning: it is intended as the sealing of the wine. From al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿĪsā, and Aḥmad ibn Jubayr al-Anṭākī, from al-Kisāʾī: a kasrah on the tā', meaning its last, like His words: ﴿and the Seal of the Prophets﴾. There is an ellipsis in it, meaning: the seal of its fragrance is musk, or its seal with which it is sealed and cut off.

**﴿from Tasnīm﴾**: ʿAbd Allāh and Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is the most noble drink of Paradise, and it is a masculine noun for the water of a spring in Paradise. Al-Zamakhsharī said: **(Tasnīm)** is a proper name for a specific spring, named Tasnīm, which is the verbal noun of sannamahu, meaning "he raised it." **(ʿAynan)** is in the accusative as an expression of praise. Al-Zajjāj said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). End of quotation. Al-Akhfash said: they are given to drink a spring (ʿaynan) **﴿from which they drink﴾**, meaning they drink it, or from it; or the verb **(yashrabu)** is implicitly made to mean **(yurwā)**, and about **(bihā)** there are several views. **(those brought near)**: Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, and Abū Ṣāliḥ said: those brought near drink it pure, and it is mixed for the righteous. [p. 443] The position of the majority is that the righteous are the companions of the right hand, and that those brought near are the foremost. Some people said: the righteous and those brought near in this verse have one meaning, applying to everyone who is given bliss in Paradise.

It is reported that ʿAlī and a group of believers with him passed by a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh, and they laughed at them and mocked them in play. Then the verse was revealed: **﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes﴾**, before ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, reached the Messenger (ﷺ). These disbelievers of Makkah are said to be: Abū Jahl, al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, and al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil. The believers are: ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb, Khabbāb, Bilāl, and others of the poor believers. The apparent view is that the pronoun in **(marrū)** refers to **﴿those who committed crimes﴾**, since in that there is consistency of pronouns for one referent. It was also said: it refers to the believers, meaning: when the believers passed by the disbelievers, the disbelievers would wink, that is, indicate with their eyes. **(jesting)**: that is, delighting in mentioning them and in laughing at them. The majority recited **(fākihīn)** with an alif, meaning possessors of jest, play, and joy at their mockery of the people of faith. Abū Rajāʾ, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah, Abū Jaʿfar, and Ḥafṣ recited it without alif. The pronoun in the nominative in **(raʾawhum)** refers to the guilty, meaning: when they saw the believers, they attributed them to error, and they were right in attributing it to them.

**﴿but they were not sent﴾** as guardians over the disbelievers. The mention of their being astray is a provocation of speech among them, and there was in the verse some gentleness (muwādaʿah), meaning: the believers were not sent to be guardians over the disbelievers. This is according to the view that this was abrogated by the verse of the sword. Al-Zamakhsharī said: and they were not sent as guardians over them, as a denial of their hindering them from polytheism and of their calling them to Islam and their striving in that. Since the mention of the Day of Resurrection had preceded, it was said: **﴿So today those who believed﴾**; and **(today)** is in the accusative governed by **(yaḍḥakūna)**, laughing at them in the Hereafter. **(observing)** is a circumstantial state of the pronoun in **(yaḍḥakūna)**, meaning they laugh while looking at them and at what they are in of humiliation and punishment after honor and bliss. Ka'b said to the people of Paradise: windows through which they look at the people of the Fire. It was also said: a transparent curtain between them through which they see their condition. **﴿Have they been rewarded?﴾**, that is, were they recompensed? It is said: **thawwaba** and **athāba** when one repays him. From it is the poet's saying:

*I will reward you, or a rewarder on my behalf will reward you, and it is enough for you that you be praised and thanked.*

This is an interrogative with the meaning of confirmation for the believers, meaning: were they recompensed for it? It was also said: **﴿Have they been rewarded?﴾** is attached to **(observing)**, and **(observing)** is governed by the sentence in a position of accusative after dropping the preposition **ilā** ("to"). The majority recited **﴿hal thuwwiba﴾** with the lām of **hal** pronounced clearly, while the two Naḥwīs (al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ) and Ḥamzah, and Ibn Muḥaysin, assimilated it into the thāʾ. In His words **﴿what they used to do﴾** there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: "a recompense or a punishment for what they used to do."
